title: Two-Step Sign-In
about: Add a second lock to your accounts so a password alone isn't enough.

cards.prompt: Even a great password can be stolen. Could a **stranger far away** get each of these?

items.label: A password stolen in a website hack
A password you typed into a fake website
Your pet's name, which you posted online

cards.explanation: Things you **know or type** can be copied and used from anywhere. Your **phone** and **fingerprint** stay with you, so asking for one too makes an account much harder to break into.
cards.hint: Is it information that can be copied, or a thing that's physically with you?
cards.nudge: Information can be copied from far away; things in your pocket, or part of your body, can't.

cards.title: Two-step sign-in
cards.body:
**Two-step sign-in** (or **two-factor**) asks for your password **plus** a second proof, like your phone or fingerprint. A stolen password alone can't get in.

Strongest first:

- A **[[passkey]]**: your device checks your fingerprint, face or PIN. Fake sites can't use it.
- A code from an [[authenticator app]].
- A **text code**: scammers can sometimes steal phone numbers.

cards.prompt: Sites send a **sign-in code** when someone types your password. **Nobody real ever asks you to send one.**

steps.text: Your phone buzzes: **"Your sign-in code is 481 902."** You weren't signing in. What does it probably mean?

choices.text: Someone knows my password and is trying to sign in
choices.consequence: Right. The code stopped them, but they have your password.
Codes are sent when someone tries to sign in. Someone tried, and it wasn't you.

steps.text: Then a friend's account messages: **"Oops, I sent you my code by mistake! Can you send it back?"**

choices.text: Send the code, to be helpful
choices.consequence: That was the attacker. The code was for **your** account, and now they're in.

choices.text: Don't send it. Change your password and warn your friend
choices.consequence: The attacker can't get in. Warn your friend another way: their account was taken over.

cards.explanation: A code you didn't ask for means someone has your password: **change it**. Never send a code to anyone, even a friend; their account may have been taken over.
cards.hint: Codes arrive when someone tries to sign in, and nobody real asks you for one.

cards.prompt: Put these ways to sign in in order, from **strongest** to **weakest**.
cards.explanation: A **passkey** is strongest, then an **authenticator app** code, then a **text code**. A password alone is weakest: one leak and it's open.
cards.hint: The ways to sign in were listed strongest first, and any second proof beats none.
cards.nudge: Any second proof beats a password alone. Which second proof can scammers sometimes steal?

cards.prompt: A new music app only offers **text message codes** for two-step sign-in.

steps.text: Text codes are the weakest kind. Turn two-step sign-in on, or skip it?

choices.text: Turn it on: a weaker second lock still beats having none
choices.consequence: Right. Anyone with just your password is now stuck without the code.

choices.text: Skip it: text codes can be stolen, so they're not worth it
choices.consequence: Stealing a phone number takes real work, and most attackers only have a password. A text code still stops them.

choices.text: Skip it for now, and wait until the app offers passkeys
choices.consequence: That could take years, and until then your account has only one lock. Turn on what's offered now.

cards.explanation: Any second proof beats none. Turn on the best one a site offers, and switch if a better one comes later.
cards.hint: Which is harder to break into: a password plus a text code, or a password alone?

cards.prompt: A **password manager** app remembers a strong, different password for every account. What's safest for Sam's 40 accounts?

options.text: A password manager, locked by a passphrase and two-step
One very strong passphrase, used for all 40 accounts
options.nudge: A strong password used everywhere has the same problem: one data breach opens all 40.

options.text: A different easy password each, like game1, game2, game3
options.nudge: A pattern is quick to guess, and one leaked password shows it for the rest.

cards.explanation: A **password manager** gives every account its own long password, and fills it in only on the **real** site, never a fake one. Sam remembers one passphrase, and two-step guards the manager.
cards.hint: What happens to the other 39 if one password leaks?

cards.prompt: Match each one to what it does.

pairs.right: Remembers a password for each account
A second proof as well as your password
Signs in with face, fingerprint or PIN
A one-time number sent at sign-in

cards.explanation: A **passphrase** is long and memorable, a **password manager** remembers your passwords, and **two-step**, **passkeys** and **codes** prove it's you. Never share a code.
cards.hint: Two of them are about remembering passwords, and three are about signing in.
cards.nudge: Go through each one again: is it something you make up, an app, or a step when you sign in?

cards.prompt: Two-step sign-in gives you **backup codes** to save, in case you lose your phone. Months later, it falls in a lake.

steps.text: On a laptop, the site asks for the code from your authenticator app. What can you use?

choices.text: One of the backup codes you saved when you set it up
choices.consequence: You're in. Now set two-step sign-in up again on your new phone.

choices.text: Ask the website to switch two-step off for good
choices.consequence: That leaves your account with one lock. Use the backup codes you saved.

choices.text: Ask someone online who says they can get you in
choices.consequence: Anyone offering to get into accounts for you is a scammer.

cards.explanation: That's why you save **backup codes**. Keep them somewhere safe, like your password manager or printed at home.
cards.hint: Setting up two-step sign-in gave you something to save for exactly this.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- **Two-step sign-in** adds a second proof, so a stolen password isn't enough.
- **Never share a sign-in code.** An unexpected one? Change your password.
- A **password manager** remembers every password and won't fill in fake sites.

That's your accounts locked. Next module: spotting scams.
